Limpopo: The Baobab Bomb

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Hundreds of thousands of indigenous trees – including baobabs and other specially protected species – are set to be the first casualties of a massive heavy industrial plan in Limpopo. It’s a scheme driven by the provincial government and Chinese developers who have touted it as the ‘ the most competitive energy metallurgy special zone in the world’.
This is the Musina-Makhado Special Economic Zone (MMSEZ) one of 9 operational zones and three planned zones, that were approved – originally by President Zuma’s government in 2017. The MMSEZ envisages two main developments, one in the northern Musina area focusing on light manufacturing and agro-processing, the other in the southern Makhado (formerly Louis Trichardt) area focusing on coal mining, coal-fired power generation and steel manufacture.

It's project that is being fought against by different sectors of the community. Three ( or two) people’s stories we will tell, who are fighting against this are:

Lauren Liebenberg, a prominent activist fighting the MMSEZ development, Lauren, her two sisters and parents are part of a private nature reserve, Herd Reserve. This development could jeopardise the biodiversity in the Unesco-designated Vhembe Biosphere Reserve in Northern Limpopo and so strike a blow for the tourism industry in the area.

And

Makoma Lekalakala( Director Earthlife Africa) who lobbied against this project .As a direct result of his efforts the United Nations Development Programme ( UNDP) withdrew their support’ saying human and environmental rights including well-being of communities must be prioritised.

And

Mphatheleni Makaulule and her organisation, Dzomo La Mupo,( the voice of Creation) a grassroots community-based organisation that has been one of the strongest and most vocal (and courageous) opponents of the planned expansion of coal mining and development of the MMSEZ in the Vhembe.

We will bring in other voices for specifics of the irregularities/controversies.
Question the powers that be in the Limpopo Province to get clarity on a project that despite it’s enormous costs seems to be flying by the seat of its’ pants

We will be examining the economic, environmental community and political implications of this enormous scheme over the coming months, drawing South African’s attention to the range of issues impacting lives and livelihoods.

We will investigate the roots of the MMSEZ, how the project is still on going:
Despite no feasibility on the project.
Despite an environmental pre -feasibility study identifying critical environmental issues (like high water requirements in a water scarce area.
Despite unexamined environmental risks a patch of SA soil has been handed over for 90 years to a foreign country. A project that will have major impact on the use of scarce resources, exports, pollution, greenhouse gas emissions ,local employment market and economic market.



Further information:
MMSEZ will cost over USD 22 billion and will be the biggest such industrial development in South Africa. The scale of the project is immense. It spans an enormous area ( 60 Km2 of the actual plant and then 100’s of km’s of land that will have to be bulldozed and trees felled) encompassing multiple industrial sites and extensive infrastructure development, ranging from power and petrochemicals plants, to a mega-dam on the Limpopo River and the so-called “Smart City” township.

The energy-metallurgical zone will more than double South Africa’s annual crude steel production capacity - and the SEZ is intended to support the development of the largely-unexploited Greater Soutpansberg Coalfield. These two aspects raise big red flags - SA historically has been unable to compete in international steel markets and exploitation of new coal deposits will significantly increase CO2 emissions and threaten SA's adherence to the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, a carbon-reduction measure imposed by the EU on all trading partners.
Arcelor-Mittel announcing the closing of their plants in South Africa points to this. Donald Mackay, specialist of South African industrial policy talks about the era of primary steel production in South Africa is not viable.

The MMSEZ is still in the planning phase but has drawn criticism from many quarters for being out of step with South Africa's commitments to reducing carbon emissions and the Just Energy Transition, as well as its negative impact on biodiversity, water security and archaeological heritage. It will create a waste land out of the entire area which is a Unesco-designated Biosphere Reserve in recognition of its outstanding biodiversity value.

Permit applications sent to the national Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) show that there are plans to destroy as many as half a million protected indigenous trees. Including Baobabs, Shepherd trees, marula’s and leadwood trees.
So far, the department confirmed that it has issued licences for the destruction of 1,000 specially protected trees but forestry officials said they would adopt a “cautious and responsible approach” when considering another application to destroy a further 9,000 protected trees.
Apart from the significant scale of biodiversity damage from tree felling, the plan to develop a new heavy industry zone in Limpopo has also raised concern about whether there is enough water and electricity available in the region to support a mega-scale scale development centred around steel smelting, coal washing and other metallurgical processes.
Water: All this land which forms part of the Vhembe District Bioreserve will be drastically impacted by the SEZ. The entire project relies on damming the Limpopo River and channeling 60% of it’s water flow to wash the coal and cool the steel. This is one of SA’s water scarce regions. The Sand river last flowed in 2014 util much needed rains swelled it with flood waters in December.
So in January on the recce the Limpopo is flowing, everything is green but even still the plans to build a mega dam to support MMSEZ will use up 60% of the Limpopo’s annual flow resulting in a dry wasteland. The down stream water will affect communities. This water will need to be pumped to the Southern site. Messina is a cess pool, no water most of the time with sewage in the streets already. Louis Trichardt or Mukhado has days without water.
There is an additional plan is to access water from Zimbabwe, but these plans very are …nothing concrete, lots of plans. And certainly no feasibility study has been done yet.
Power: Their own experts said we cannot have a coal fired station and meet climate change expectations – Paris Accord.
So the next plan was using renewable energy
Their own energy expert says it’s impossible to run this plant in this huge big economic zone on solar alone. The battery storage will take up half the space – too BIG
So they are going back to the idea coal fired stations

Another Legal issue challenge Limpopo Department of Economic Development, Environment and Tourism (Ledet) is acting as both developer and referee in the environmental approvals process.
The applicant and the decision maker.
How can a non -prejudiced Environmental Impact Assessment be done when they can fire you if it’s not what LEDET wants.
In fact a previous EI A practitioner was fired for not reporting what they wanted to hear.

Kirsty Youens Attorney : We are saying LEDET has failed to consider the Climate Change Assessment Report Or the Energy Assessment Report. Had it done so it would have noted Climate Change and Energy rated extremely High even after mitigation. And mitigation of climate change impact is not possible without limiting the Coal Fired Power Station from the project. NB despite the report acknowledging serious impact on climate and…emissions still . authorized it.

Current status:
Planned clearance of 9,000 trees has apparently begun with aerial photos showing bulldozers on site.. This will be the site of the Makhado Colliery, the flagship metallurgical zone. The Limpopo Economic Development Agency has applied for the clearance of up to 650,000 trees in total including many baobabs more than 1000 years old.
We flew over the affected area where we see an enormous stretch of pristine bushveld already cleared of its trees ..is to be strip mined for coal which will fuel and iron ore smelter.

There has been EIA for this specific clearing. Which is another legal issue.

Deidre Carter CEO of Agri Limpopo spoke about this when I met her:
We cannot allow them to do what they are trying to do not only from an environmental aspect but this piecemeal approach. Fencing off an area and getting an EIA on just a specific area without going into the bigger picture.
EIA which are being bulldozed through by the Premier. She has a recording of him saying if we don’t get a good EIA we will fire him and get another EIA which gives us the go ahead,

A good example of the piecemeal approach is the Sand Mine which is on Sand River There is a loophole in the law that says if you want to mine sand on less than 5 hectares you don’t need a permit/mining license So one EIP linked to MMSEZ issued 17 applications under his name, right next to each other, each only 5 h this is the type of fraud they are seeing in the agriculture communities.

This is of the legal challenges called ‘Project Splitting’
Areas that clearing has already began partly due to the piecemeal approach MMSEZ is taking doing EIA’s on small sections of land without reference to the bigger picture.
You have a big – possibly controversial project – and to make it easier to get environmental authorization, you piecemeal process…without factoring in the massive development itself

No E I A done for the Smelter that will happen somewhere in the future
OR Power Plant also happen somewhere in the future.
So devastating areas without the whole plan

Lindy Wilson DA Leader of the Province
This is not an ANC project it is a Chinese project with an offer to the ANX to make it work
She has been connecting the dots as projects come to their attention in the province.
There are plans for a speed train from Gauteng to Polokwane. ‘Hilary Construction’ had road contracts to upgrade the roads in this area, a big contract was suddenly cancelled and granted to a Chinese company
An small unused airport is suddenly being upgraded.

There have been memorandums of understanding between Messina Municipality and Zimbabwe….to bring water in to supply water to SEZ…never in her life has she heard about a municipality making international trade deals with another country never mind another municipality. Checked with Attorney Kirsty Youens who confirms a province should not be doing international trade deals this should be done on the international stage, I will also check with parliament

What is still a concern
Limpopo is deeply impoverished area and this, according to proponents, maybe their only shot at development. There is a promise of 20 000 jobs first 5 years not necessarily local job. This is not a guarantee, Chinese developers have no obligation to employ a % of the local community.
But No alternative development models have been adequately explored;
Rural development is the key to economic growth, but we need to consider the socio-economic sustainability of the models we choose. What is happening here is clearly incompatible with the surrounding landscape and communities and there are several more environmentally friendly and nature based alternatives to consider.

Like Agriculture, Deidre Carter says there has been no consultation or discussion re how increasing the agricultural capacity would be better. Huge underdeveloped market for citrus and tomato, is a small successful agro industry presently which could be expanded.

Lauren Liebenberg: Bio Diversity, Tourism and Agriculture are 40% more efficient at generating jobs than the mining and industry
According to analysis by Living Limpopo, the value of the biodiversity and carbon credit yield from the creation of the proposed Great Vhembe Conservation Area potentially exceeds the risk-adjusted value of the economically recoverable coal reserves.
As an added bonus of this competing land-use scenario, no dedicated power is needed, no water resources will be depleted, no pollution and environmental degradation will result, no damage will be done to the agricultural and tourism sectors and no harm will be caused to human health, or to the food and water security of poor, land-dependent communities or to our cultural heritage.
Cath Vise from Endangered Wild Life Trust
Vhembe Region is the last connecting corridor linking Mapungubwe to Greater Kruger Regions…this allows species to move ..this will create an impenetrable block. We need to be able to ensure that we keep our corridors open.

Mpathaleni (Dzomo La Mupo) and Dr Sarah Venter: Baobab Foundation : The destruction of the baobabs.– sacred trees – this is the emotional tug at the story
How important baobabs are, hot spots of biodiversity and different uses.
Sarah pioneered the development of a baobab fruit export industry in Vhembe and undertook an assessment, estimating that the fruit of the 65000 baobab
and marula trees that will be destroyed by the MMSEZ could sustainably support 2700 seasonal jobs and 118 permanent jobs per year, generating R6.7 billion ($351 million) for local communities over the next 30 years.

Possibly …John Rosmarin of Leshiba Wilderness been heading up conservation planning periodic review in the Vhembe Biosphere reserve. A requirement of UNESCO. He talks how this has been violated (LEDET) and there has been a vested conflict of interest that has severely prejudiced conservation and sustainable development in the Vhembe Biosphere Reserve. The next periodic review will only be due in 2029, by which time the MMSEZ and many of the coal mining projects might will have been approved and operational, irreversibly damaging the environment.

Script:


Lauren: It’s very hard to put into words but you know it’s my own memories that go back to when I was young.
Mphatheleni: [SUBS] Trees in Venda… When we have trees we are at home.
Lauren: It’s one of the last truly wild places in Africa, in South Africa,
Mphatheleni: [SUBS] My name is Mphatheleni. That’s my name. Mphatheleni means “build for me”. Build for me what is getting destroyed.
VO: Two women fighting the potential destruction of an area spanning 10’s of thousands of hectares.
Lauren: It has just somehow ended up being my crusade to save the Vhembe…
Mphatheleni: [SUBS] We are claiming our land because it is our home.
Link: Hundreds of thousands of indigenous trees including baobabs and other specially protected species are said to be the first casualties of a massive heavy industrial plan in Limpopo.

VO: This is the most northern part of South Africa – the Vhembe district. Stretching from the Kruger National Park in the east, to Blouberg Nature Reserve in the western side of Limpopo Province.
Lauren: The Vhembe is an area that is of enormous biodiversity significance.
VO: For Lauren Liebenberg, this area sits at the very core of her being.
Lauren: Nature has value. The trees growing rooted in the soil have value…

VO: Trees like the iconic Baobab and Marula, and thousands of protected species form part of this unique landscape… and in 2009 it was declared a UNESCO Biosphere reserve, supposedly giving it special protection.

VO: At the heart of this region lies the Soutpansberg mountain range … and at its foothills … the Soutpansberg Coal Fields…
Lauren: Ultimately it has been 100% about coal.
VO:10 years ago the Limpopo government hatched a plan to exploit these enormous undeveloped coal deposits.
Lauren: It always will be about the development of the Greater Soutpansberg coal field and the extraction of those coal resources.
VO: It’s a project driven by the Limpopo Department of Economic Development, Environment and Tourism – LEDET – and Chinese investors… and is known as the Musina Makhado Special Economic Zone, or MMSEZ.
Lauren: We first found out about the Musina Makhado Special Economic Zone the old fashioned way, read about in the newspaper…
VO: The MMSEZ will span 2 different zones – A Northern section earmarked for industrial manufacturing …and in the South, a steel smelter.
Lauren: I can still remember my sense of utter disbelief - They are going to be building an industrial mega project here in the Vhembe in the biosphere reserve.
VO: They will use the coal from the Soutpansberg region, and iron brought in from the Northern Cape - 1 000 kms away - to make steel for the local and export market.
V/O Lauren established ‘Living Limpopo’- an advocacy group to consolidate the objections from the diverse communities across the Province;
Lauren: It was the shock that jolted us into action and thousands of people responded and registered their objection to this.
Dr Sarah Venter: It’s the only part of South Africa where you actually get naturally occurring baobabs
VO: Dr Sarah Venter has spent years researching the Baobab.
Dr Sarah Venter: To just cut these trees down, it's removing hundreds of different species that rely on this tree for a short term, heavy industrial plant that will only last 30 years…
Deidre: We didn’t have answers on the impact it’s going to have on our underground water …I mean we don’t have water even if you go to the towns the taps are dry.
VO: Deidre Carter, heads up AgriLimpopo – which looks after the interests of commercial farmers in the province.
Deidre: We did object. That was in February 2022. It took them 5 months to actually acknowledge receipt of the e-mail and then they sent us a letter to say well your appeal has been rejected.
V/O: The MMSEZ has been met with fierce opposition. Appeals and legal challenges have resulted in work stoppages and cost overruns.
Lauren: This is the now abandoned construction site for the north site of the MMSEZ. You’re looking at 200 million rands of taxpayer money being wasted…

VO: …Flying over Limpopo you can see other areas where clearings have started and then had to stop..
[pause]
Mphatheleni: Musina Makhado Special Economic zone is an evil thing to destroy life. It’s about destroying, killing killing to the last.
V/O Mphatheleni Makaulule comes from a long lineage of deep indigenous spiritual knowledge. She has been celebrated across the world for the work she has done for communities. Ironically in her province- the place she lives – her wisdom has been ignored.

Mphatheleni: There will be no air to breathe, there will be no more water to drink. It will be dirty, dirty.
Masa: They say that this Special Economic Zone is going to provide economic opportunities, it’s going to bring jobs to people…

Mphatheleni: Creating jobs for whom? For how long? How many jobs? Which skills do the people of Vhembe have to do those jobs? How much are they going to earn?

V/O: Across the province, unemployment is rife, so the promise of jogs has significant attraction
Lindy: 20 000 jobs is wonderful, but for who and at what level? Are we just going to say we’ve employed 10 000 labourers on this site?
V/O: Lindy Wilson is head of the DA in Limpopo
Lindy: Do we have the skills in South Africa that are going to be ignored because it’s a foreign investment and they want to bring their skills rather than using our own. So, when it comes to employment, you’ve got to look at a whole cross section of what this project requires.
HOD Matodzi Rathumbu: All other industries, whether it’s tourism and agriculture has not been able to absorb this larger the army of unemployed which is around 500 000.
V/O: Head of Department at LEDET – Matodzi Rathumbu- adds that it’s Government’s obligation to provide employment.
Masa: It’s a protected area. How are you going to protect that pristine land?
Matodzi Rathumbu: When you look at the biosphere it has got 3 stratas that is the core which Is a protected area which you will not touch especially around issues of industrialization.
VO: Limpopo’s provincial and national parks make up the core conservation areas of the Biosphere reserve. Then there are buffer zones between these core areas and where the development is taking place.
Matodzi Rathumbu: If you Look at our SEZ it is not in the core, it is not in the buffer, it is in the transitional space.
V/O: In other words, LEDET believes that because the development will be outside the core and buffer zones impact on protected species will be minimal. But LEDET has been accused of ignoring -or even suppressing- the updated Vhembe Bioregional plan which shows far larger Core and Buffer areas – an allegation they have repeatedly denied.
VO: Visiting Limpopo while they’re experiencing a record amount of rain, might give a different picture, but water scarcity is a reality in the province… and steel production is water intensive.
Matodzi Rathumbu: In the Short term we will use the Bore Holes .And then the 2nd Phase, the Zimbabwe Government has agreed they will share their water with Messina Mukhado SEZ
VO: The agreement with Zimbabwe is for an annual 15 million cubic metres of water, specifically for the town of Musina. Not nearly enough for the thirsty Special Economic Zones as well.
And the long-term plan is to build a storage dam along the Limpopo River
Lauren: This plan threatens the resilience of the entire Limpopo River Basin system, and all those dependent on the water resources.

VO: A pipeline will need to be built – from the proposed dam – to feed the southern zone.

Lauren: They will be pumping the water uphill a distance of about 50 kms to the site of the smelter.

V/O: But it’s not just water and environmental concerns that are making people angry. While LRDET is propelling this development, the implementation is in the hands of a department subsidiary – LEDA – the Limpopo Economic Development Agency. So LEDA appoints the specialists who assess the environmental impact, but final approval lies with LEDET

Masa: You are the regulator and you are also the implementing agent
Matodzi Rathumbu: No we are not
Masa: But as a department..this MMSEZ will be under you thats correct right?
Matodzi Rathumbu: It is under Limpopo Economic development Agency, it is not under us.
V/O LEDA though falls directly under LEDET
HOD:
Masa: But aren't you refereeing your own match?
Matodzi Rathumbu: Not at all.Not at all
V/O: He may not agree, but the fact remains LEDET will ultimately have final say over crucial issues like the potential environmental impact of this project
[pause]
VO: The MMSEZ is billed as South Africa’s largest ever industrial development, and is based on an economic development model from a different era… with its very uncertain outcome, it has already cost us.
Lauren: You have to look at the very real risk that we’re just building a future stranded asset in the bushveld.
V/O: In a response to parliamentary questions from the DA, Trade and Industry Minister, Parks Tau, answered that over half a billion has already been spent from the billion allocated for the medium term.
Lindy: 10 years on and all we have done is bulldoze an area of ground. This project has already cost a billion rand on what?
Masa: Where has money so far gone because you haven't started building?
Matodzi Rathumbu: There are operational costs. Then there is a budget for capital expenditure which has got to do with infrastructure, installation, utilities and other out of office expenditure.
Masa: How many trips has been taken, how much money has been spent?
Mathodzi: If you have investors outside your borders in order to consult with them either they will come to you or you will go to them isn’t it?. To equate going on an international mission and benchmarking with feeding a poor person I don’t agree with that logic.
VO: And then, in a final blow, we find out that in the southern zone - where operation’s had been suspended because of a court appeal -…… strip mining has started, illegally, behind closed gates. The beginning of the future Makhado Colliery.
Masa: Well, Looks like it’s already started
V/O: The damage may already have been done, potentially impacting the integrity of the entire biosphere.

Mphatheleni :If they are doing that… yes they can undermine, they can ignoreand do that… but It’s in the hands of the ancestors ….to use the name of Makado to destroy Venda land. AAAH

Lauren: It has just somehow ended up being my crusade to save the Vhembe… Mphatheleni: [SUBS] We are claiming our land because it is our home. VO: At the heart of this region lies the Soutpansberg mountain range … and at its foothills … the Soutpansberg Coal Fields… Lauren: Ultimately it has been 100% about coal. VO:10 years ago the Limpopo government hatched a plan to exploit these enormous undeveloped coal deposits. Lauren: It always will be about the development of the Greater Soutpansberg coal field and the extraction of those coal resources. VO: It’s a project driven by the Limpopo Department of Economic Development, Environment and Tourism – LEDET – and Chinese investors… and is known as the Musina Makhado Special Economic Zone, or MMSEZ. [pause] Mphatheleni: Musina Makhado Special Economic zone is an evil thing to destroy life. It’s about destroying, killing killing to the last. V/O: Across the province, unemployment is rife, so the promise of jogs has significant attraction Lindy: 20 000 jobs is wonderful, but for who and at what level? metadata.Summary: Hundreds of thousands of indigenous trees – including baobabs and other specially protected species – are set to be the first casualties of a massive heavy industrial plan in Limpopo. It’s a scheme driven by the provincial government and Chinese developers who have touted it as the ‘ the most competitive energy metallurgy special zone in the world’. This is the Musina-Makhado Special Economic Zone (MMSEZ) one of 9 operational zones and three planned zones, that were approved – originally by President Zuma’s government in 2017. The MMSEZ envisages two main developments, one in the northern Musina area focusing on light manufacturing and agro-processing, the other in the southern Makhado (formerly Louis Trichardt) area focusing on coal mining, coal-fired power generation and steel manufacture. It's project that is being fought against by different sectors of the community. Three ( or two) people’s stories we will tell, who are fighting against this are: Lauren Liebenberg, a prominent activist fighting the MMSEZ development, Lauren, her two sisters and parents are part of a private nature reserve, Herd Reserve. This development could jeopardise the biodiversity in the Unesco-designated Vhembe Biosphere Reserve in Northern Limpopo and so strike a blow for the tourism industry in the area. And Makoma Lekalakala( Director Earthlife Africa) who lobbied against this project .As a direct result of his efforts the United Nations Development Programme ( UNDP) withdrew their support’ saying human and environmental rights including well-being of communities must be prioritised. And Mphatheleni Makaulule and her organisation, Dzomo La Mupo,( the voice of Creation) a grassroots community-based organisation that has been one of the strongest and most vocal (and courageous) opponents of the planned expansion of coal mining and development of the MMSEZ in the Vhembe. We will bring in other voices for specifics of the irregularities/controversies. Question the powers that be in the Limpopo Province to get clarity on a project that despite it’s enormous costs seems to be flying by the seat of its’ pants We will be examining the economic, environmental community and political implications of this enormous scheme over the coming months, drawing South African’s attention to the range of issues impacting lives and livelihoods. We will investigate the roots of the MMSEZ, how the project is still on going: Despite no feasibility on the project. Despite an environmental pre -feasibility study identifying critical environmental issues (like high water requirements in a water scarce area. Despite unexamined environmental risks a patch of SA soil has been handed over for 90 years to a foreign country. A project that will have major impact on the use of scarce resources, exports, pollution, greenhouse gas emissions ,local employment market and economic market.

Mpathaleni (Dzomo La Mupo) and Dr Sarah Venter: Baobab Foundation : The destruction of the baobabs.– sacred trees – this is the emotional tug at the story How important baobabs are, hot spots of biodiversity and different uses. Sarah pioneered the development of a baobab fruit export industry in Vhembe and undertook an assessment, estimating that the fruit of the 65000 baobab and marula trees that will be destroyed by the MMSEZ could sustainably support 2700 seasonal jobs and 118 permanent jobs per year, generating R6.7 billion ($351 million) for local communities over the next 30 years. Possibly …John Rosmarin of Leshiba Wilderness been heading up conservation planning periodic review in the Vhembe Biosphere reserve. A requirement of UNESCO. He talks how this has been violated (LEDET) and there has been a vested conflict of interest that has severely prejudiced conservation and sustainable development in the Vhembe Biosphere Reserve. The next periodic review will only be due in 2029, by which time the MMSEZ and many of the coal mining projects might will have been approved and operational, irreversibly damaging the environment.
